title: Wildlife, netting and protected-species boundaries
audience: Pond and water-feature technicians who install or check netting, do edge work and work near wildlife
learningOutcomes: Identify common pond wildlife and the situations where wildlife protection rules may apply
Install or check netting so that it protects fish without trapping or harming wildlife
Stop work and refer when nests, eggs, breeding animals or protected species are found
Explain the limits of this lesson: it does not authorise handling, moving or harming native animals, or disturbing their nests and eggs

instruction.heading: Ponds attract wildlife
instruction.body: Ponds attract birds, frogs, dragonflies, water beetles, turtles, snails and many other animals. Many pond animals use the very shallow water at the edge, where the water is only a few centimetres deep, and well-vegetated ponds can look dry to a person while still supporting these animals. Some of the animals are common, and some are native species that may be protected. A heron may be a threat to fish, but it is a native bird and its protection status depends on the state and the species. Do not assume that a species is common, and do not assume that a rule does not apply because the pond is in a backyard. Native animals are protected under state and territory law (for NSW), and listed threatened species and communities may also be protected under national law.

instruction.heading: What the state and national rules say
instruction.body: Under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016, NSW's native birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals count as protected, with the dingo as the stated exception. The state department can grant licences to people or organisations that control, hold or trade protected species, and the page lists bird exceptions in some regions, such as sulphur-crested cockatoos and galahs in several Local Land Services regions. At federal level, threatened species and communities on the official lists are a protected matter, and a proposed action that could significantly affect them goes to the federal environment minister for a decision.

instruction.heading: Netting and its risks
instruction.body: Netting is used to keep birds away from fish. It must be supported above the water, secured at the edges and tensioned so that it does not drop into the pond, where birds, frogs or turtles can become tangled. Loose, torn or sagging netting is a trap for wildlife. Check netting at each visit, according to the owner's plan, and look for animals caught in it. If an animal is trapped, do not handle or release it unless you are authorised and competent to do so. Otherwise, report the entrapment to the owner and to the appropriate wildlife authority. Keep the netting clear of the water surface so that animals can still reach the edge, and secure the edges so that the net cannot be pulled into the water.

instruction.heading: Nests, eggs and breeding animals
instruction.body: Frogspawn, bird nests, eggs, young animals and breeding sites are not to be moved, removed or disturbed by a contract worker. If you find one, pause work in that area, keep the disturbance low, and tell the owner. Record the location and the observation. Work in that area may resume only when the owner and the wildlife authority's guidance allow it, and work elsewhere should continue only if it does not disturb the animals.

instruction.heading: What this lesson does not authorise
instruction.body: This lesson does not authorise you to handle, capture, relocate, kill or harm native animals, to disturb protected habitat, or to remove or relocate frogspawn or nests. Completing this lesson does not give that authority, and it does not give any licence to hold, trade or control protected animals.

procedure: Check whether wildlife is present in or around the pond before starting netting or edge work.
Pause work and inform the owner if nests, eggs or breeding animals are found, and record the location.
Install netting above the water and secure it at the edges, with no sagging sections.
Check netting for entrapment at each visit, according to the owner's plan.
If an animal is trapped, report it to the owner and the wildlife authority unless you are authorised and competent to free it.
Record the location, the observation and the action taken.

workedExamples.situation: A netting installation is due at a pond, and a frog's eggs are visible under the edge stone where the net will be fixed.
workedExamples.reasoning: The technician does not move or remove the eggs. The edge work in that area pauses, the owner is told, and the wildlife authority's guidance is sought before the work in that area resumes. The technician records the location and the observation. Netting is fitted in other areas only if the owner agrees and the work does not disturb the eggs.

workedExamples.situation: A bird is found tangled in loose netting at a pond the technician visited last week.
workedExamples.reasoning: The technician does not handle or release the bird unless authorised and competent. The owner and the wildlife authority are informed. The netting is secured to prevent further entrapment, and the event is recorded with the time and the position of the netting. The check frequency is raised as the owner's plan allows.

equipmentAndPpe: Netting and fixings suited to the pond, with no sagging sections
Contact sheet for the owner and the relevant wildlife authority
Gloves and PPE as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Moving frogspawn or a nest to clear the work area.
commonErrors.prevention: Pause the work, inform the owner and seek the wildlife authority's guidance.

commonErrors.error: Leaving loose netting that traps birds or frogs.
commonErrors.prevention: Secure and tension the netting, and check it at each visit.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a native species is common or unprotected.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the rules for the species and the state before any action.

commonErrors.error: Handling or releasing a trapped animal without authority.
commonErrors.prevention: Report to the owner and the wildlife authority unless you are authorised and competent.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: In New South Wales, native birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals count as protected under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016, with the dingo as the stated exception. This lesson does not grant that authority.

Under the national law, threatened species and communities on the official lists are a protected matter, and a proposed action that could significantly affect them goes to the federal environment minister for a decision. This lesson does not grant any approval.
A trapped animal can injure the person handling it, and it may be stressed. Use gloves, and avoid direct contact unless authorised.

qualityStandard: Netting is supported above the water, secured at the edges and free of sagging sections
Work pauses when nests, eggs or breeding animals are found, and the owner is told
No wildlife is handled, moved or released without authority
documentationEvidence: Observation of wildlife or nests, with location and the action taken
Report to the owner or the wildlife authority where an animal was trapped
summary: Many pond animals are native and may be protected, so do not assume a rule does not apply.
Netting must be supported, secured and checked for entrapment at each visit.
Pause work near nests, eggs and breeding animals, and seek guidance.
This lesson does not authorise handling, relocating or harming wildlife, and it does not grant any licence or approval.

knowledgeChecks.question: A frog's eggs are found under the stone where netting is to be fixed. What is the correct action?
options: Move the eggs to another pond nearby, since the water there is clean and safe for them
Pause work in that area, tell the owner, and seek the wildlife authority's guidance
Fix the net over the eggs right away, since the net will keep them safe from birds
Remove the stone and bin the eggs, since they are in the way of the netting work

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is loose netting a problem at a pond?
options: It makes the water warmer on sunny days
It changes the pH of the water
It can trap birds, frogs or turtles
It stops the pump from running

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about this lesson is correct?
options: It authorises relocating native animals from the pond to the creek
It grants a wildlife handling authority for the owner's staff
It covers all state rules completely for every wildlife issue
It does not authorise handling, relocating or harming native animals
